items.title: What makes rock deep beneath continents break away and sink?
items.summary: We usually picture mountain building as rock being pushed upward. But deep beneath some mountain belts and volcanic arcs, the opposite can happen: dense rock at the base of the crust can become unstable, break away and sink hundreds of kilometers into the mantle, dragging part of the rigid outer shell of the Earth (the lithosphere) with it. Seismic images suggest that this process, known as lithospheric dripping, has occurred beneath the central Andes and California's Sierra Nevada.

items.title: The secret of 'strange metals' may lie in quantum statistics, not collisions
items.summary: In an ordinary metal, electrons behave like well-defined particles that occasionally bump into imperfections or vibrations of the crystal. Many materials with strong electron–electron interactions, including the copper-oxide (cuprate) superconductors, break these rules. In these "strange metals," electrical resistance rises in a straight line with temperature over a very wide range. Electrons seem to lose their momentum at the fastest rate quantum mechanics allows, the so-called Planckian limit. What causes this is still an open question.

items.title: Imaging nerves during surgery without turning down the lights

Surgeons may therefore need to dim or switch off the room lights during fluorescence imaging, interrupting normal surgical workflow.
